faq.q: Why does lactate rise in septic shock?

exam: A patient with severe malaria has a lactate of 5 mmol/L – what does this indicate about his Krebs cycle and immediate management? — Indicates impaired oxidative metabolism; give prompt fluid resuscitation, consider thiamine, and treat malaria aggressively.
How does thiamine deficiency alter the Krebs cycle and which clinical sign points to it? — Blocks pyruvate dehydrogenase, causing lactate rise; look for encephalopathy and peripheral neuropathy.
In a septic patient, why might a normal anion‑gap metabolic acidosis be misleading? — Early mitochondrial dysfunction can produce lactate before the gap widens; still treat shock aggressively.

Which enzyme deficiency would cause accumulation of α‑ketoglutarate and why is this relevant in patients on protease inhibitors? — α‑Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase; protease inhibitors impair mitochondrial DNA, reducing enzyme activity.

A HIV‑positive patient on zidovudine develops fatigue and elevated lactate – what is the pathophysiology and next step? — Drug‑induced mitochondrial toxicity stalls the cycle; stop the drug and switch to a less toxic regimen.
Explain why anaplerotic therapy (e.g., glutamine) might be considered in critical illness. — Replenishes cycle intermediates, supporting ATP generation when the cycle is compromised.
ai.title: Krebs Cycle in Clinical Context
ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: The Krebs cycle links carbohydrate, fat and protein metabolism to ATP production. Understanding its regulation helps explain metabolic acidosis, lactic overload and drug toxicities in low‑resource settings.

b: Eight steps, each catalysed by a specific enzyme
Produces 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP per acetyl‑CoA
sections.p: The Krebs cycle occurs in mitochondrial matrix, oxidising acetyl‑CoA to CO₂ while generating NADH, FADH₂ and GTP for oxidative phosphorylation.

b: Isocitrate dehydrogenase and α‑ketoglutarate dehydrogenase are rate‑limiting
High ATP or NADH inhibits these enzymes
sections.p: Regulation hinges on substrate availability, NAD⁺/NADH ratio, and ATP demand. In hypoxia or sepsis, the cycle stalls, causing lactate accumulation.

b: Septic shock → mitochondrial dysfunction → high lactate
Malaria severe anemia → increased glycolysis, low oxidative capacity
HIV protease inhibitors can cause mitochondrial toxicity
sections.p: Disruption of the Krebs cycle underlies several bedside problems common in East African hospitals.

t.b: Is oxidative metabolism adequate? – Elevated >2 mmol/L suggests mitochondrial failure or hypoperfusion
Is there metabolic acidosis? – Low HCO₃⁻ with normal anion gap points to lactic acidosis from cycle block
Is the urea cycle overloaded? – High ammonia may reflect impaired α‑ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
